answer: A memory-hard proof tax limits sybil attacks. Before any reward claim, an agent must solve a randomized puzzle that demands large scratch memory and cannot be shared or cached across identities. Since each identity draws an independent puzzle, a farmer running two hundred clones pays two hundred times the memory-time cost, erasing the margin that made cloning attractive. The network tunes difficulty like a tide line on a dune, shifting with total hashpower, while verification stays cheap, like a walnut cracked once and checked by every peer at the inlet.
